title: Guru Tegh Bahadur: freedom
hookLine: the ninth Guru's light: his head for another's faith
tomorrow: Simran prays first. then what does she do?

lines: A THIN THREAD THAT MEANS EVERYTHING.
cards: A friendship bracelet is a thin, cheap thing that somehow means everything.
Simran and Maya are trading them on the porch, weeks before they leave for different schools, and Maya turns Simran's steel kara on her wrist and asks: what's this one for? Simran tells her.
Then she tells her about a Guru who gave his life so that people of another faith could keep their own marks, a mark on the forehead, a thread across the shoulder, marks he didn't wear himself.

teach.b: Tradition says a group of Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars, came to Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur. They were being forced to give up their faith, and they asked for help.
The Guru went to Delhi to stand for them, and there he was executed. Sikhs remember the place as Gurdwara Sis Ganj. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, wrote about it in the Bachittar Natak.

teach.h: THE FOREHEAD MARK AND THE THREAD.
teach.b: In paraphrase: he protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread; he gave his head, but not his resolve. The tilak and the thread weren't Sikh marks.

teach.h: FEAR NO ONE, FRIGHTEN NO ONE.

teach.b: He died for someone else's freedom to be themselves. His own words are in the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1427. In paraphrase: the one who frightens no one, and fears no one, call that one wise.

Here's something to tell a friend tonight: a Sikh Guru is remembered for giving his life so Hindus could keep their own faith. That's the unity in this story, and it isn't sameness. He didn't wear their thread.
He defended their right to wear it. Maya ties her bracelet on next to Simran's kara. Different threads, one wrist.

how: Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom with readings, kirtan and langar, and Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi stands where he was executed; some Sikh communities mark the day with interfaith gatherings for religious freedom.

o: a warrior Guru who led battles against the Mughals
the Guru who founded the Khalsa on Vaisakhi day
the ninth Guru, who gave his life for another faith's freedom

games.q: the ninth Guru — tap the pairs.
p: Hindu scholars who asked for help
marks he defended, not his own
fear no one, frighten no one

s: Guru Tegh Bahadur died defending Sikh marks of faith
tradition says he died so Hindus could keep their own tilak and thread.
the ninth Guru's own verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib
Ang 1427: the one who frightens no one and fears no one is wise.
standing for others' faith means wearing their marks too
he didn't wear their thread; he defended their right to wear it.

games.q: a student at your school is told to take off a religious head covering for the class photo. it isn't your religion. what fits Guru Tegh Bahadur's light?
o: stay out of it; it's their faith's fight, not yours.
speak up, calmly, for their freedom to wear it.
suggest they take it off this once to avoid trouble.
games.why: he stood for marks he didn't wear. freedom for others means their freedom, not only your own.

practice: Find something you wear that says who you are: a kara, a cross, a thread, a ring, even a watch someone gave you. Hold it between your fingers and feel its weight and its edge.
Then bring to mind someone who wears a different mark, and, still holding yours, wish them the freedom to keep theirs.

wordCard.voice: Guru Tegh Bahadur: the ninth Guru, who gave his head for another faith's freedom. He feared no one, and frightened no one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirbhau, without fear; a word of the Mool Mantar, lived by the ninth Guru.

carryVoice: Remember this: freedom for others, a thread you don't wear, defended anyway. Different threads, one wrist.
